report.summary: 6 of 14 modelled personas reach the end of the funnel with a plan they would keep; 8 leave at a named stage, most of them before the product itself is even reached. The single most expensive defect is not in the engine: it is that the route from the front page to a personal answer is longer than the patience of the people who need it most.

sections.title: Where the model says people stop
sections.body:
- **arrives** — 4 persona(s): career-changer-teacher, ld-manager-team, parent-limited-hours, reentry-career-break
- **first-five-seconds** — 1 persona(s): slow-network-student
- **understands-what-it-is** — 0 persona(s): —
- **sees-it-is-for-them** — 1 persona(s): screen-reader-user
- **trusts-it-enough-to-try** — 0 persona(s): —
- **reaches-a-real-answer** — 2 persona(s): school-student-phone, working-dev-cloud
- **reasons-to-come-back** — 6 persona(s): mech-engineer-switching, architect-specialist, self-taught-skeptic, bootcamp-instructor, grad-student-ml, tech-writer-amplifier

The concentration at *arrives* is the honest headline of this exercise: the product's problems on the funnel are dominated by the fact that nothing here creates demand, which no amount of interface work fixes.

sections.title: What the survivors have in common
sections.body:
Every persona that stays does so for the same measured reason: **zero interactions to a personal answer, with no account**. That is the asset.

The second reason is dispositional rather than technical: the personas with the highest modelled reach are the ones who reward a product for refusing to fake social proof and for naming its own limits.

sections.title: The five things that cost the most
sections.body:
**The route from the front page to a personal answer is longer than the patience of the people who need it most** (severity 64, costs 8 persona(s))

Measured: 3, against a zero-interaction answer once the person reaches the gap screen. The friction is entirely in the path, not in the product.

*Fix:* Point the primary action straight at the answer; keep guided onboarding as the secondary path.

**Most modelled personas have no measured way to arrive at all** (severity 25, costs 4 persona(s))

4 of 14 personas arrive only through channels nothing in this build demonstrates: search indexing, an app store, or social reach. The product can be excellent and still be used by nobody, because nothing here creates demand.

*Fix:* Treat distribution as a product feature: a hosted demo on a real domain, a public repository with the run instructions, and presence where these people already ask the question.

**Controls below the 36 px target the rest of the app already meets** (severity 20, costs 3 persona(s))

Measured: 22 interactive elements under 36 px in the first screen at 1440×900, while the 360 px layout passes the existing suite. The inconsistency is in the desktop chrome, not in a component library.

*Fix:* Raise header and first-screen controls to the same minimum height used elsewhere.

**The hero leads with the abstraction, not the outcome** (severity 10, costs 2 persona(s))

The measured headline is "Plan an engineering path as a graph, not a checklist" and the longest paragraph above the fold explains that the 3D scene is not live data. Both are true and neither is what a stranger needs first: what it is, who it is for, and what an answer looks like.

*Fix:* Rewrite the first screen as: outcome, audience, one real number, one action.

**A metered connection pays for a 3D hero it did not ask for** (severity 5, costs 1 persona(s))

Measured: 497 of script and a 2052 ms LCP on a 1.6 Mbit/s link. Nothing about the planning answer needs the scene; the scene is the most expensive part of the first impression.

*Fix:* Detect save-data or an effective 2G/3G connection and render the static hero, keeping every number identical.

sections.title: What the model cannot tell you
sections.body:
- It cannot say whether people will use this. It can only say which claims are legible, where the friction is, and which assumption drives which result.
- The persona parameters (patience in seconds, clicks tolerated, what each cares about) are judgement, not measurement. Change one and a verdict can flip; every verdict in the JSON records the facts it leaned on so you can check the chain.
- Nothing here models social dynamics: no reviews, no word of mouth compounding, no competitor, no seasonality.
- Six of fourteen personas never arrive through a channel that exists today, so their downstream verdicts are hypothetical by construction.

stages.quote: Someone would have to hand me this — I would not find it on my own (word of mouth from a teacher).
It was there in 0.4 s. Nothing to complain about.
"Plan an engineering path as a graph, not a checklist" — a graph is how you built it, not what I get. I had to read three lines to find out it plans a career.
22 controls in the first screen are smaller than a fingertip. For me that is not a detail, it is the difference between using it and not.
No testimonials, no ratings, no "trusted by" logos. That is oddly reassuring.
Once I am on the right screen it answers instantly — but getting there cost me 3 clicks, and I give a new site 2.

caveats: Model, not research: 14 personas with declared parameters, deterministic rules over 30 measured facts. No real people were observed.
Severity and reach are modelled weights, not measurements of any population.
The fact sheet is a snapshot of one build under declared throttling; a different device, region or build moves the numbers.
Six personas have no measured arrival channel, so their journeys are conditional on an assumption that they get there at all.
